what_it_does: When one thread of a program needs to tell another thread 'something happened' — say, a network packet arrived or a timer fired — the fastest modern approach is for the waiting thread to sit in a tight loop constantly checking a shared variable (called polling), which wastes a full CPU core just waiting. Intel added a hardware feature called User Interrupts (UIPI) that lets user-level code (ordinary programs, not the operating system kernel) send and receive such notifications without kernel involvement, similar to how a phone can ring to interrupt what you are doing rather than requiring you to constantly check the screen. However, UIPI has correctness gaps and cannot match polling latency in practice, and it lacks support for preempting (forcibly pausing) a thread from user space, kernel-bypass timers, or forwarding notifications to attached accelerator chips. xUI proposes four hardware additions to fix these gaps: a way for senders to confirm delivery, a mechanism for user-level runtimes to preempt threads without calling the OS, a timer that fires directly without OS involvement, and a path to forward interrupt signals to co-processors.
